strengths: The paper presents a rigorous differential-geometric formulation: the cotangent-lifted embedding/reduction pair (Props. 1-2) is shown by construction to satisfy both the symplectomorphism condition (7) and the projection properties (4), which is a genuine advance over soft-constrained symplectic autoencoders and linear/quadratic symplectic projections.

Comprehensive and well-designed ablations: the AE architecture (linear vs. quadratic SMG vs. weakly-symplectic AE vs. geometric AE, Table 2), the latent HNN parameterization (SPD vs. Cholesky vs. black-box), the integrator (Strang-symplectic vs. leapfrog vs. RK4 vs. Euler), latent dimension trade-offs, and joint vs. sequential training are all carefully isolated.

Evaluation spans three systems of increasing dimensionality (15-DoF pendulum, 90-DoF particle vortex, 600-DoF damped cloth), including conservative, non-separable, and dissipative cases, with both quantitative errors and qualitative long-horizon generalization beyond the data support (e.g., 625x longer horizon on the cloth).

Reproducibility treatment is unusually thorough: full architectural details, initialization schemes, learning rates, dataset generation procedures, and evaluation wall-clock times (Table 5) are provided in the appendices.
The paper demonstrates that HNNs can be extended beyond their established 2-5 DoF regime, addressing a recognized scalability limitation of Hamiltonian neural networks.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: most components are assembled from prior work, including the constrained AE (Otto et al., 2023), biorthogonal manifold optimization and SPD networks (Friedl et al., 2025), structure-preserving MOR theory (Peng & Mohseni, 2016; Buchfink et al., 2023), and the Tao (2016) augmented-Hamiltonian integrator. The core new technical contribution is essentially the cotangent-lifted symplectic AE, and the paper reads more as a careful system integration than a fundamentally new method.

The experimental scope is narrow: all three benchmarks are simulations with canonical symplectic form and known quadratic kinetic-energy structure (except the vortex), which aligns exactly with the architectural priors. Notably, the 15-DoF pendulum dataset is synthetically generated by composing a known latent 3-DoF system with a symplectomorphism, guaranteeing the submanifold structure the method assumes, which biases the comparison in its favor. No real-world data, no non-canonical systems (deferred to future work), and no comparison to learned-coordinate alternatives such as the neural symplectic form (Chen et al., 2021).

Missing a plain (non-symplectic) autoencoder + latent dynamics baseline, which would isolate the benefit of the symplectic constraint from that of nonlinear dimensionality reduction itself; the weakly-symplectic AE partially serves this role but satisfies the projection properties.

Some quantitative evidence is thin: several tables report only 10 test trajectories with large standard deviations, and improvements over the strongest baselines (e.g., SPD vs. ground-truth dissipation in Table 4) are within or near error bars.

The limitations discussion is sparse; assumptions such as a globally valid canonical chart, known additive separability of the latent Hamiltonian, and the need for ground-truth external inputs during cloth training (for the conservative variant) deserve explicit treatment.
No explicit statement about code release, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameters.

strengths: The paper is technically careful and well-written: the geometric formulation of structure-preserving MOR (Sec. 2.2) is clearly presented, and the symplecticity of the cotangent-lifted embedding and reduction is proven in Propositions 1 and 2, including the nontrivial condition (9) on the differential of the embedding.

The architecture is coherently constructed from hard geometric constraints throughout: a biorthogonally-constrained symplectic AE (guaranteeing conditions (7) and (4) by design), SPD networks for the mass-inertia and damping matrices, and a structure-preserving Strang-symplectic integrator (Tao, 2016) for the non-separable latent Hamiltonian.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough: the AE architecture (linear/quadratic SMG vs. weakly-symplectic vs. geometric AE, Table 2), latent HNN parameterization (SPD vs. Cholesky vs. black-box, Figs. 3 and 8), integrator choice (Fig. 3-middle/right), joint vs. sequential training (Fig. 14), and latent dimension sweeps are all systematically examined, and each design choice is empirically justified.

Reproducibility is strong: appendices D–G give complete implementation details (architectures, initializations, learning rates, training horizons, dataset construction), and the Riemannian optimization procedure and manifold operations are specified in closed form.

The experiments genuinely address the stated gap: HNNs are applied to systems with up to 600 DoF, far beyond the 2–5 dimensional scope of most prior HNN literature, with both conservative and dissipative dynamics.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core components are all assembled from prior work — the cotangent-lifted symplectic embedding is adapted from Sharma & Kramer (2024) and Friedl et al. (2025), the constrained biorthogonal AE is taken from Otto et al. (2023), the SPD networks are from Friedl et al. (2025), and the integrator is from Tao (2016). The contribution is essentially a Hamiltonian analog of Friedl et al.'s Lagrangian reduced-order framework, applied to HNNs rather than LNNs. The most closely related prior method (Friedl et al., 2025) is cited as motivation but never compared against empirically, which makes it hard to assess the actual added value of the proposed approach over the state of the art.

The experimental systems are favorably constructed. The 15-DoF pendulum is deliberately generated by symplectically transforming a known 3-DoF latent system, so the ground truth is exactly reducible to d=3 — an idealized setting unlikely to hold for real high-dimensional systems. All experiments are simulated, and the method requires full-state (q,p) observations, i.e., access to both positions and conjugate momenta, which is a strong assumption that precludes image-based or partially observed data (the setting motivating much of the HNN literature).

The dissipative cloth experiments require measured external constraint forces τ_c as inputs (Sec. 4.3, App. G.3), which further weakens the claim of learning 'unknown' dynamics non-intrusively; the dissipative model is only learned because damping forces are provided separately in the ablation setup.

Evidence for long-horizon stability is thin: the cloth prediction horizon is only 0.5s against a 0.3s training horizon (Fig. 5), the particle vortex test uses 10 trajectories, and results are reported as mean ± std over only 10 test trajectories with large variances (e.g., Table 2, Table 4). There is no statistical significance analysis.

The 'scale' claim is modest in absolute terms: 600 DoF with d=10 latent dimension is meaningful but far from intrinsically high-dimensional systems such as continua or fluids invoked in the introduction, and no scalability analysis (e.g., training cost, scaling behavior of the Strang-symplectic integration through the doubled augmented phase space) is provided beyond small runtime table 5.

Several central claims rest on qualitative evidence: generalization 'beyond the data support' and physical consistency are demonstrated primarily with trajectory plots (Figs. 2, 5, 9, 11) rather than quantitative long-horizon or energy-conservation metrics across all systems; the energy analysis (Fig. 13) covers only the cloth case.

There is no explicit limitations section; limitations (canonical form assumption, full phase-space observability, known external forces, simulation-only validation) are either deferred to future work or left unstated, and no code release is mentioned, which limits practical reproducibility despite detailed documentation.

strengths: Strong geometric foundations: the paper derives the cotangent-lifted embedding and proves (Props. 1-2) that the biorthogonally-constrained AE yields a symplectomorphic embedding satisfying both the symplecticity condition (7) and the projection properties (4), giving hard architectural guarantees rather than soft penalties.

The method systematically integrates several structure-preserving components (constrained biorthogonal AE, SPD networks for mass-inertia and damping matrices, Riemannian Adam, and Tao's Strang-symplectic integrator for non-separable Hamiltonians) into a coherent framework, with careful treatment of the Riemannian geometry of the parameter spaces.

Experiments cover three systems of substantially higher dimension (15, 90, 600 DoF) than the 2-5 dimensional systems typical of prior HNN work, including a dissipative case with external constraint forces, and demonstrate generalization well beyond the training horizon.

Thorough ablations isolating each design choice: the symplectic AE vs. linear/quadratic SMG projections and weakly-symplectic AE (Table 2), geometric vs. Cholesky vs. black-box HNN (Fig. 3, Tables 3-4), integrator choice (Fig. 3), joint vs. sequential training, and latent dimension sweeps. Wall-clock runtimes (Table 5) are a welcome addition.
Extensive appendices with dataset generation, architectures, hyperparameters, and derivations support reproducibility, and the proofs are largely self-contained.
weaknesses: The main benchmark appears favorably constructed: the 15-DoF pendulum is generated by composing a latent 3-DoF system with a known symplectomorphism (App. G.1.1), so an exact 3-dimensional symplectic ROM exists by construction, matching the chosen latent dimension. This weakens the claim that the method 'scales Hamiltonian learning to high-dimensional systems'; the vortex and cloth experiments partially mitigate this but use only 10 test trajectories and (apparently) single training runs without seed variance.

Baselines are mostly internal ablations. The paper builds directly on Friedl et al. (2025) (SPD networks, biorthogonal Riemannian optimization) and Sharma & Kramer (2024)/Buchfink et al. (2023), but does not compare against the corresponding full-dimensional or Lagrangian ROM baselines on equal footing on the cloth, nor against other learned ROM approaches (e.g., Shi et al., CHNN, Lagrangian operator inference of Sharma et al. 2024, which is cited). This makes it hard to gauge the magnitude of the advance over the closest prior art.

Novelty is incremental: each component exists in prior work (Otto et al. 2023 constrained AE, Sharma et al. 2024 cotangent lift, Friedl et al. 2025 SPD networks and Riemannian training, Tao 2016 integrator). The main new element is the proof of symplecticity of the lifted biorthogonal AE plus the joint architecture, which is valuable but modest.

The explanation for why the geometric HNN beats the black-box HNN on the vortex (Sec. 4.2, 'the AE learns a symplectomorphism to a latent space where the Hamiltonian can be decomposed') is speculative and not verified, since the vortex Hamiltonian (40) provably does not separate into kinetic and potential terms, contradicting the assumed quadratic form (11).

The method requires full state observations (positions and momenta, plus external forces in the dissipative case) on a manifold with a global canonical chart, which limits applicability relative to observation-based approaches and to systems with non-canonical or global charts; the paper defers non-canonical forms to future work and has no explicit limitations section.

Training cost is significant (multi-step loss integrated through the Strang splitting for H steps via Riemannian Adam), but only inference runtimes are reported; a training-cost comparison would strengthen the practical case.

Minor presentation issues: a blank page (p. 11), Fig. 1 is dense and hard to parse, and several claims (e.g., 'outperforming traditional HNNs and state-of-the-art reduction approaches') are stronger than the specific comparisons provided.
